content: Tamberly Freight runs 260 refrigerated trucks out of three depots in the English Midlands.
Until July 2026 our route planner ran once a night, at 02:00, and drivers received the next day's routes on a printed manifest.
In July we replaced the nightly batch with an event-driven planner that re-plans a route whenever an order is added, cancelled or delayed.
Each change is published to a message queue, and the planner recomputes only the routes that touch the affected depot.
The results after eight weeks: the average time from an order being placed to it appearing on a driver's route fell from 19 hours to 40 minutes.
Empty running, the share of kilometres driven with no load, dropped from 23 percent to 17 percent.
We considered buying a commercial routing service instead.
We rejected it because none of the three vendors we spoke to supported temperature-zone constraints, and every one of our loads has one.
The migration took a team of five engineers eleven weeks.
Printed manifests are still produced as a backup and will be retired in January 2027.

Card payments through Quillon failed for 47 minutes on 4 September, from 14:12 to 14:59 UTC.
Roughly 18,000 transactions were declined; the exact figure will change as merchants report retries.
Our leading hypothesis is that a certificate rotation on the card-network link at 14:10 left one of three gateway nodes presenting an expired certificate.
We think this is likely but have not reproduced it.
We have ruled out a database fault: the payments database showed normal latency throughout.
It is unclear why traffic was not drained from the affected node automatically.
The health check may have been testing the wrong endpoint, but we have not confirmed that.
A full review will be published by 30 September.
No customer card data was exposed.

The collapse it describes is usually dated to 1841, but no newspaper report of it has been found.
